title: Real Estate Finance II: Markets, Loans & Programs
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: The secondary mortgage market exists primarily to:
options: Originate loans directly to consumers
Buy existing loans so lenders can replenish capital and lend again
Set interest rates for all residential mortgages
Insure lenders against borrower default
rationales: Origination happens in the primary market, between lender and borrower.
Correct. The secondary market purchases existing loans, recycling lenders' capital and keeping mortgage money available — which is also why a borrower's loan is often sold shortly after closing.
Rates are set by market forces and individual lenders, not by the secondary market directly.
Insuring against default is the role of PMI, FHA, and VA guarantees.

questions.stem: Which entity GUARANTEES securities backed by government loans rather than purchasing loans itself?
options: Fannie Mae
Freddie Mac
Ginnie Mae
The Federal Reserve
rationales: Fannie Mae purchases conventional loans and packages them into securities.
Freddie Mac likewise purchases loans for securitization.
Correct. Ginnie Mae is a government corporation that guarantees timely payment on securities backed by government loans such as FHA and VA — it guarantees rather than buys.
The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and does not guarantee mortgage securities in this role.

questions.stem: A $1.6 million loan on a Pasadena home that exceeds Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchase limits is BEST described as:
options: A government loan
A conventional, non-conforming (jumbo) loan
A conforming loan
An FHA loan
rationales: Government loans are FHA, VA, and similar insured or guaranteed products.
Correct. It is conventional because no government agency insures or guarantees it, and non-conforming because it exceeds the conforming loan limit — the definition of a jumbo.
Conforming means the loan meets Fannie/Freddie standards, including the size limit, which this loan exceeds.
FHA loans are government-insured and subject to county loan limits.

questions.stem: Private mortgage insurance (PMI) on a conventional loan protects:
options: The borrower, if they lose their job
The lender, against borrower default
The seller, against a failed closing
The property, against physical damage
rationales: PMI provides no benefit to the borrower despite being paid by the borrower.
Correct. PMI protects the lender against loss from default and is generally required when the loan-to-value ratio exceeds 80%.
Sellers are not protected by mortgage insurance.
Physical damage is covered by hazard insurance.

questions.stem: The Federal Housing Administration's role in an FHA loan is to:
options: Lend the money directly to the borrower
Insure the loan made by an approved lender
Guarantee a portion of the loan for veterans
Purchase the loan on the secondary market
rationales: FHA does not lend; approved private lenders make the loans.
Correct. FHA insures loans made by approved lenders, which enables lower down payments and more flexible credit standards.
Guaranteeing loans for veterans is the VA's function.
Purchasing loans is the function of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

questions.stem: Which is a distinguishing feature of a VA loan compared with FHA and conventional financing?
options: It requires a 20% down payment
It typically requires no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance
It is available to any first-time buyer
It carries no fees of any kind
rationales: VA loans generally require no down payment at all.
Correct. Eligible veterans typically finance 100% with no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee applies (waived for certain disabled veterans).
Eligibility is limited to qualifying veterans, service members, and certain surviving spouses.
A funding fee applies to most VA loans, though it may be financed.

questions.stem: Under the CalVet program, the state:
options: Insures a loan made by a private lender
Guarantees a portion of a conventional loan
Purchases the property and sells it to the veteran under a contract of sale
Provides a down payment grant to the veteran
rationales: Insuring private loans describes FHA, not CalVet.
Guaranteeing a portion of a loan describes the VA program.
Correct. CalVet buys the property and resells it to the veteran under a contract of sale, retaining legal title until the contract is paid — a structure unlike an ordinary loan.
CalVet is a financing structure, not a grant program.

questions.stem: A buyer purchases at $685,000 with $96,000 down. The loan-to-value ratio is approximately:
rationales: 80% would require a $137,000 down payment on this price.
Correct. Loan = 685,000 − 96,000 = 589,000; 589,000 ÷ 685,000 = 0.8598, or about 86% — above 80%, so PMI would be required on a conventional loan.
14% is the down payment percentage, not the loan-to-value ratio.
90% would correspond to a loan of $616,500.

questions.stem: A buyer takes a $540,000 loan and pays 2.5 discount points plus a 1 point origination fee. The total charged in points is:
rationales: $13,500 covers only the 2.5 discount points, omitting the origination fee.
$5,400 is a single point.
Correct. One point = 1% of the loan = $5,400. Discount: 2.5 × 5,400 = 13,500. Origination: 5,400. Total = $18,900.
$21,600 corresponds to 4 points, one more than the 3.5 charged.

questions.stem: Points on a real estate loan are calculated as a percentage of the:
options: Purchase price
Loan amount
Appraised value
Down payment
rationales: Using the purchase price is the most common error on this calculation.
Correct. One point equals 1% of the loan amount, not of the price, value, or down payment.
Appraised value affects LTV, not the computation of points.
The down payment is unrelated to points.

questions.stem: A loan factor table shows $6.32 per $1,000 for a 30-year fixed loan. On a $472,000 loan, monthly principal and interest is:
rationales: Correct. 472,000 ÷ 1,000 = 472 thousands; 472 × $6.32 = $2,983.04 in monthly principal and interest.
$3,614.71 is the full PITI once monthly taxes and insurance are added.
$298.30 misplaces a decimal.
$2,360.00 corresponds to a $5.00 factor.

questions.stem: A loan whose payments are less than the interest accruing, causing the balance to increase, has:
options: Full amortization
Negative amortization
A prepayment penalty
A balloon payment
rationales: Full amortization retires the entire balance by maturity.
Correct. In negative amortization the unpaid interest is added to principal and the balance grows — a structure that contributed to the 2008 crisis and is now sharply restricted.
A prepayment penalty is a charge for paying early, unrelated to a growing balance.
A balloon payment is a lump sum at maturity on a partially amortized loan.

questions.stem: An ARM has a 2.75% margin, a 2% periodic cap, and a current rate of 5.25%. At adjustment the index is 4.75%. The new rate will be:
rationales: $7.50% is the fully indexed rate (4.75 + 2.75) before applying the cap — the classic distractor.
Correct. The fully indexed rate is 7.50%, but the 2% periodic cap limits the increase from 5.25% to a maximum of 7.25%, so the cap binds.
4.75% is the index alone, without the margin.
10.25% is the lifetime ceiling (5.25 + 5), not this adjustment.

questions.stem: In an adjustable-rate mortgage, the component the lender does NOT control is the:
options: Margin
Index
Periodic cap
Adjustment period
rationales: The margin is the fixed percentage the lender sets and adds to the index.
Correct. The index is a published market rate outside the lender's control; index plus margin equals the fully indexed rate.
Caps are negotiated loan terms set at origination.
The adjustment period is a term of the loan agreement.

questions.stem: An agent's social media post reads: 'Own this Ontario home for just $2,100/month!' Under Regulation Z, stating that payment amount:
options: Is exempt because social media is not regulated advertising
Is a trigger term requiring disclosure of additional credit terms
Requires only the APR to be stated
Is permitted if the agent adds 'approximately'
rationales: Regulation Z applies to advertising regardless of medium.
Correct. A stated payment amount is a trigger term, requiring the ad to disclose the additional required credit terms — general claims like 'low payments' avoid the trigger.
More than the APR alone must be disclosed once a trigger term appears.
Softening the number with 'approximately' does not remove the trigger.

questions.stem: The three-business-day right of rescission under Truth in Lending applies to:
options: A purchase-money loan on a buyer's new home
A refinance or equity loan secured by the borrower's principal residence
Any loan on investment property
All FHA and VA loans
rationales: Purchase-money loans used to buy a home are specifically excluded from the rescission right.
Correct. The right of rescission applies to certain refinances and home equity loans secured by the borrower's principal residence.
Investment property loans are outside the principal-residence protection.
The rescission right depends on the loan's purpose and the property's status, not the program.

questions.stem: A lender offers an agent $500 for each buyer referred who closes a loan, calling it a 'marketing fee.' Accepting this payment would:
options: Be lawful, because it is labeled a marketing fee
Violate RESPA's prohibition on payment for referrals of settlement services
Be lawful if disclosed to the buyer in writing
Be lawful if the agent also posts about the lender online
rationales: The label does not control; the substance is compensation for referrals.
Correct. RESPA prohibits giving or accepting anything of value for the referral of settlement service business; only payment for services actually performed at fair market value is permitted.
Disclosure does not cure a prohibited referral fee.
A token marketing activity does not convert a per-closed-loan payment into compensation for actual services.

questions.stem: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits a lender from denying credit because:
options: The applicant's debt-to-income ratio is too high
The applicant's income comes from public assistance
The applicant has a recent bankruptcy
The property fails to appraise
rationales: Debt-to-income is a legitimate underwriting factor.
Correct. ECOA prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or because income derives from public assistance.
Credit history, including bankruptcy, is a permissible underwriting consideration.
Insufficient collateral value is a legitimate basis for denial.

questions.stem: A seller carries back an all-inclusive trust deed that wraps an existing loan containing a due-on-sale clause. The PRIMARY risk is that:
options: The buyer cannot record the AITD
The underlying lender may accelerate the existing loan upon the transfer
The seller loses the right to receive payments
The AITD automatically becomes a first lien
rationales: An AITD can be recorded; recording is not the problem.
Correct. The transfer can trigger the underlying loan's due-on-sale clause, and the buyer also risks losing the property if the seller stops paying the underlying loan despite receiving payments.
The seller continues to receive payments under the wrap note.
The AITD is junior financing; it does not displace the existing first lien.

questions.stem: California's usury limits generally do NOT apply to a loan that is:
options: Made between family members
Arranged by a licensed real estate broker
Secured by commercial property
Under $50,000
rationales: Family relationships create no usury exemption.
Correct. Loans made or arranged by a licensed real estate broker are generally exempt from California's usury limits — one practical reason hard-money lending flows through brokers.
Property type alone does not create the exemption.
No general small-loan exemption based on that amount applies.
